newsitem.title: USA: Top U.S Rep sees balanced budget amendment in spring.
newsitem.headline: Top U.S Rep sees balanced budget amendment in spring.

text.p: House of Representatives Budget Committee chairman John Kasich said on Sunday he expected to see a balanced-budget constitutional amendment next spring.
Kasich, speaking on the Fox News Sunday television programme, said he believed enough Democrats supported an amendment to achieve the necessary votes to pass the legislation.

The Ohio Republican said there would be room for some exceptions to a balanced budget, in times of depression or war, but no "escape clauses" which Republicans fear President Bill Clinton wants to insert.

"Obviously if there's a national calamity you want an escape clause (if) you end up in a depression or in a time of war," said Kasich. "But we don't want to have convenient excuses being used to circumvent the need to balance the budget."

Last week Clinton said he could live with an amendment to the Constitution requiring a balanced budget if it provided for exceptions when the economy was in recession. Later, Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said the president still strongly opposed any balanced budget amendment.

Said Kasich: "If you listen to a lot of the Democrats, and when it gets down to whether they will favour a balanced budget amendment which the public overwhelmingly favours, I think we will come up with the votes. I anticipate we will do this sometime around the spring.
If the amendment clears Congress on the required two-thirds vote of each chamber, it will have to be ratified by three-fourths of the state legislatures.

Kasich said the process of reaching a balanced budget amendment would also produce an agreement on Medicare, the health programme for the elderly. Clinton accused the Republicans during the presidential campaign of seeking to cut Medicare to pay for tax cuts.
"I anticipate we will reach some agreement on Medicare and we will probably end up with some commission to make the more structural changes," said Kasich.

"Both sides recognise the need for structural changes (to Medicare). The question is how we get them. The public is tired of all the back and forth. Let's see if we can reach an agreement on a whole host of issues, lay down a plan to balance the budget by 2002 and then move on."
